newsitem.title: USA: DuPont halts plans for mine near swamp.
newsitem.headline: DuPont halts plans for mine near swamp.

text.p: Faced with growing criticism, the DuPont Co said Friday it was suspending indefinitely its plans to mine titanium ore from land adjacent to the Okefenokee Swamp, one of the largest wilderness areas east of the Mississippi.

The company had planned to begin surface mining along the border of the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge in 2002. DuPont said it would ask a respected, independent third party to help address environmental concerns.
"We are stopping activities related to our proposed mining operation," Ellen Kullman, vice president and general manager of DuPoint White Pigment and Mineral Products, said.
"We will not go forward unless and until we can satisfy all participants and ourselves that we will not harm the Okefenokee refuge."

Kullman said DuPont took the action because of "strong positions" that had been taken in the past week. During an April 3 visit to southeast Georgia, Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt said the mine was "not an appropriate neighbor for a national wildlife refuge."

Joe Beverly, board chairman of the Georgia Department of Natural Resources, said he planned to ask the state not to approve the mine until there is "a clear and convincing demonstration" that it will not cause irreparable harm.
DuPont said it would "immediately engage in an intensified and expanded collaborative process with key environmental groups, government bodies and local citizens."

Kullman said the 38,000 acres DuPont has purchased and leased next to the 438,000-acre swamp had the largest deposit in the country of titanium ore. The company uses the mineral to manufacture titanium dioxide, a white pigment used in paint, paper, toothpaste and cookie fillings.

Much of the swamp is designated as a wilderness area home to endangered and threatened species such as the indigo snake, the red cockaded woodpecker and the wood stork. Alligators and mosquitoes are plentiful and the refuge is one of the few remaining areas where the Florida black bear is found.
The swamp is known worldwide as the home of the Pogo comic strip drawn by Walt Kelly.
Environmental groups oppose the mining, saying it would affect the swamp's water table and cause particulate air pollution that would ruin the swamp and nearby wetlands.
